explanation: "Although" joins the subordinate clause "Although I love to cook" to the main clause, so it is a (subordinating) conjunction. It is not a preposition because it is followed by a full clause with its own subject and verb, not by a noun phrase.
"Lazy" describes the noun "dog", so it is an adjective. A word sitting between the article/other modifiers and the noun it qualifies is almost always adjectival.

"Still" here modifies the verb "lives", telling us that the action continues up to now, so it is an adverb (of time). "Still" can be an adjective meaning motionless (still water), but that sense does not fit here.

"Array" here means fine attire or dress; it follows the article and adjective ("a costly array") and is the object of the preposition "in", so it is a noun. "Array" can also be a verb (to array oneself), but there is no verb slot for it in this sentence.
"Terrifying" qualifies the noun "accident", so it is an adjective (a present participle used adjectivally). It is not a verb here because it has no subject and carries no tense.
"Encounter" is the object of the preposition "in" and is preceded by "a police", so it functions as a noun. "Encounter" is also a verb (to encounter danger), but not in this position.

"This" stands alone as the subject and points out a particular person, which makes it a demonstrative pronoun (this/that/these/those). It would only be a demonstrative adjective if a noun followed it, as in "this friend".
"Always" modifies the verb phrase "get up", telling how often the action happens, so it is an adverb of frequency.
"Very" modifies the adjective "beautiful", not the noun "car", so it is an adverb (of degree). Remember that adverbs can modify adjectives and other adverbs, not just verbs.
"Wow!" expresses sudden emotion and stands outside the grammar of the sentence, marked off by an exclamation mark, which is the definition of an interjection.
The fixed collocation is "abhorrence of" (compare "a horror of", "a hatred of"). The verb takes a different pattern - you abhor something with no preposition - so "to" and "at" are traps.

"Upon" and "on" imply contact with the roof, which cannot follow "flew", so the choice is between "over" and "above"; the added phrase "soaring high in the sky" stresses height rather than crossing, which is the job of "above". "Over" is the tempting answer and would be right for simply passing across the roof ("the bird flew over the roof and away").
"Acquit" always takes "of": one is acquitted of a charge or of an offence. "Acquitted on all charges" is heard in journalism, but the grammar-book answer expected here is "of".

Before a gerund expressing the thing hoped for, the idiom is "confident of winning" (like "sure of winning", "hopeful of winning"). "Confident in" is also good English but is used of the thing you trust - confident in her ability, confident in himself - not of the expected outcome.

"Decide on" is the ordinary idiom for settling a choice - I have decided on my course of action. Note honestly that option (b) "upon" is equally correct English (decide on/upon are listed together in standard grammars), so this item has two defensible options; "on" is the commoner form and the safer pick.

Traditional appropriate-preposition lists (Wren & Martin and the like, which these papers follow) give "excel in" for a field or activity - he excelled in painting, in mathematics. "Excel at" is acceptable modern usage, especially before a gerund, so this is not a clean single-answer item, but "in" is the expected key.

"Must be mailed" states a deadline, and the preposition for a deadline is "by" - i.e. not later than Monday. "On Monday" is grammatical but would name the exact posting day rather than a limit, and "until" wrongly suggests the mailing continues up to Monday.
The fixed adjective-plus-preposition pattern is "intent on (doing something)" - he is intent on repeating his attempt. No other preposition follows "intent" in this sense.
"Sparing of" is the standard idiom for being economical with something - sparing of words, sparing of praise, sparing of expenditure. "In" may look natural but is not the collocation tested here.
You have confidence "in" a person or thing - confidence in you and your abilities. "Confidence on/upon" is a common Indian-English slip and "with" is simply wrong here.

"Every Friday" signals a repeated habit, which takes the simple present, and the third-person singular subject "Mr. John" needs the -s form: drives. "Is driving" would describe something happening now, not a weekly routine.

Her studying was in progress at the moment John arrived, so the past continuous "was studying at the library" is right. "Had studied" would wrongly place the studying as finished before he arrived, and "has been studying" clashes with the past-tense narrative.

This is the classic past continuous plus past simple pattern: a longer action in progress (was crossing) is interrupted by a sudden one (struck). "Had been crossing" would need a second, later past reference point to be interrupted from, which the "when" clause does not supply.

"By the time the show began" fixes a point in the past, and the duration "for more than half an hour" runs up to that point, which calls for the past perfect: had been. "Have been" would measure up to the present instead.

The cooking was finished before the past moment of arriving and discovering, so the past perfect "had prepared" is needed. Simple past "prepared" would suggest the two events happened at the same time, and the present perfect forms clash with the past-tense sentence.

"The children" is plural, so the plural present form "cheer" is the only fitting option. "Cheers" is singular, "was cheering" has a singular verb with a plural subject, and "will cheered" is ungrammatical as printed - the natural "were cheering" was simply not offered.
